title: Ryan Colton introduced as UNH athletic director - WMUR
content: Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Ryan Colton was officially introduced as the new Athletic Director at the University of New Hampshire on Tuesday. Colton comes from the University of Richmond, where he was a deputy athletic director and chief of staff. The Massachusetts native returns to New England. He previously worked at Holy Cross and Providence College. "There's a lot of passion. You can feel it," Colton told News 9 Sports. "I feel like we can really harness that to build something special here, but the road ahead for intercollegiate athletics, especially at this level, is going to be a difficult one." Colton says financially supporting the athletic department is at the front of his mind. "I'm really looking forward to working with advancement folks on campus to learn how I can engage with with our top supporters to support Wildcat athletics. We're going to also look at how we can increase revenues from a commercial perspective as well. We really need to dive in and set a plan and a strategy moving forward," Colton said. title: UnitedHealth (UNH) Stock Slips As Medical Cost Fears Mute Profit Rebound - simplywall.st
content:
UnitedHealth Group just delivered a punchy earnings headline while the stock quietly slipped. Shares closed at US$402.20, down about 1.6% on the day and modestly weaker over the past month, even as quarterly adjusted earnings per share landed at US$6.38 and operating earnings rose sharply compared with a year ago. The market looks more cautious than the numbers alone might suggest. Investors seem to be discounting the earnings strength and raised full year guidance, and instead leaning into lingering concerns about medical cost trends. The rest of this report unpacks whether that caution fits the full story in the latest results. Love UnitedHealth Group's earnings power but concerned about medical cost trends dragging on the story? Bulls argue UnitedHealth Group is in an operational recovery where Medicare Advantage, Optum and AI tooling steadily rebuild earnings power. Q2 gives that view real but specific support. Adjusted EPS of US$6.38 and a 55% rise in operating earnings show the cost and benefit redesign work is flowing through the income statement. Medicare Advantage looked healthier than the narrative of structural damage suggested. Management now expects 2026 Medicare margins above 3% and a smaller enrollment decline than feared, which lines up with the plan to trade volume for profitability. OptumHealth reported better care management and higher margins, with AI now embedded in about 70% of employed providers. The 86.7% medical care ratio, helped by US$860 million of favorable prior period development, points to tighter execution, although part of that help is non recurring clean up rather than pure run rate improvement. Bears focus on stubborn medical cost pressure, fragile commercial margins and heavier regulatory risk around vertical integration. Q2 does not clear those issues. Commercial medical cost trend is still described as “stubbornly high,” and now sits above the roughly 11% level the company had planned for. That delays the hoped for recovery to around 7% commercial margins and shows that benefit redesign and pricing are not yet fully offsetting provider coding intensity, specialty drugs and use of the dispute resolution process. Medicaid margins remain in a small loss range for 2026, so not every government program is fixed. On top of that, the fresh push from Senator Warren’s Patients Before Monopolies Act and the broadened DOJ antitrust work keep break up and litigation risk live. The stock’s 1.6% drop on the day of the report suggests investors are still treating these as active overhangs. title: Ty Miles is UNH's lineman of many skills - UnionLeader.com
content: Ty Miles played in each of the University of New Hampshire’s 13 games last season, and if he looked out of place it was for good reason. Miles, who graduated from Londonderry High School, lined up as an interior offensive lineman in practice last year, but was used exclusively as a tight end on game day. “I started a couple games, but it was at tight end mostly blocking,” Miles explained Monday during the team’s annual media day. “Nothing technically on the O line. None of those guard, center or tackle spots. I was playing tight end the whole time. “I would play center, guard and tackle in practice, but then when it was game time I would end up playing tight end. I had a couple routes. They never threw it to me though.” Versatility is one of Miles’s strengths. He’s been playing primarily guard and tackle on the right side of the line this summer as the Wildcats prepare to open their CAA season at Albany on Friday, Aug. 28. He said he has no preference between guard and tackle. “Athletically, I feel like I’ve always been great outside playing tackle, but I can still move inside and get guard reps,’ he said. “Either way I feel great at both positions. “Still kind of determining where I’m going to be going into the season. Still trying to earn that spot. That’s where I’m sitting at right now.” Miles, a 6-foot-5, 315-pound junior (academically), wore No. 91 early in his UNH career, but will wear No. 72 this year. He was No. 75 when he played at Londonderry. “The good thing about Ty is he’s versatile,” UNH head coach Sean Goldrich said. “You can move him around a bunch of different positions. At this point in camp we’re moving the final pieces to make sure we find the best five that fit, but he’s going to play somewhere for us at a high level. “He’s been awesome to work with. He’s another blue collar, tough, gritty kid who just shows up and works every day. He has a lot of good football in front of him.” As a freshman, Miles didn’t get any game action until the final four games of the regular season. That was by design so he could preserve his redshirt season. He was allowed to play in UNH’s FCS playoff game against UT Martin without burning his redshirt. “I was still a little bit behind physically back then, I felt,” Miles said. His playing time increased last season, but the UNH coaching staff clearly felt he was most valuable when the team lined up in multiple tight end sets. That staff is gone, as former head coach Rick Santos left UNH to become the head coach at Penn during the offseason. Goldrich hired all new assistants when he was hired to replace Santos. Miles said his decision to remain at UNH following the coaching change was a good one. “We showed up here for spring with a new staff and it was great,” he said. “We had a team meeting, kind of setting that standard that nothing was going to change. The goals were still the same, just different people running it. “This new coaching staff is young, but they keep the energy high. The staff is great. I’m super glad I made the choice staying here with them and trusting them because everything they’ve been doing is very promising for the future.” © Copyright 2026 Union Leader Corp., P.O. title: UNH launches 3-year degrees amid proposed USNH leadership changes - InDepthNH.org
content:
InDepthNH.org (https://indepthnh.org/2026/08/10/unh-launches-3-year-degrees-amid-proposed-usnh-leadership-changes/) DURHAM — Amid a proposal that would see the positions of University System of New Hampshire (USNH) chancellor and the University of New Hampshire (UNH) president merged into one role, UNH now offers a way to earn certain applied bachelor’s degrees with 90 credit requirements in three years, and save up to $10,000 in tuition costs. The UNH College of Professional Studies (CPS) announced that it is now offering two new programs: the online Applied Bachelor of Science in Management and Applied Bachelor of Science in Computer Information Technology degrees. Both programs are currently open for enrollment, with a start date for classes beginning on Aug. 31. The CPS offers open-rolling admission and admits students five times per year. “There are two programs; one is in the field of Management, and one is in Computer Information and Technology. They’re applied bachelor’s programs, meaning they are less than the traditional 120-minimum credit. We launched these two to really meet what we’re hearing from students and employers that we need affordable, accessible opportunities,” Tamara VonGeorge, associate vice provost for online learning at UNH said. She also noted, “With our current undergraduate tuition rate, and the reduction from 120 to 90 credits, it’s a little over $10,000 (that students will save) … It’s a savings in tuition, but it’s also being able to achieve your career goals sooner by having that degree earned sooner.” VonGeorge continued that the programs will be completely virtual (online), and the target audience is “working adults, military students, transfer students, or folks who are trying to earn a bachelor’s degree while they are engaging in other activities, primarily the workforce.” The faculty also took the time to redesign the programs so that it wasn’t just “going in and reducing the number of credits. They really looked at what students need to know and be able to do,” she explained. VonGeorge also noted that the students enrolled into these new programs will get reassurance that they’re receiving the same level of academic quality that students in traditional 120-credit courses receive. She said they went through the university’s accreditor — New England Commission of Higher Education (NECHE) — which reviewed the programs and determined they met all the foundational requirements. “We have a student outcomes assessment in place where we are evaluating these programs to hold students to the same (standard as students in 120-credit courses), we expect the same level of outcome out of these students… Our faculty have aligned the curriculum with the program learning outcomes in the same way that they would for any degree program. We’re not doing this differently, we’re doing it through the same curricular processes and the same faculty oversight that we would in any degree program,” VonGeorge said. VonGeorge added that experiential learning opportunities were built into the programs, which could provide internships for students looking to gain hands-on experience. She also noted the programs were built to be transfer-friendly, and that these programs “are a really good opportunity for students to build on what they already know (and) what they’ve already learned, and to be able to really focus on that area they want to learn.” “It gives those students the opportunity to really dig deep in what it is they’re interested in learning about,” she said. When asked about what the student response has been like so far, she said: “It’s still early; we’re still getting the word out. Our advisors are starting to hear from folks who are interested. I think it’s really an opportunity for people to explore, and think about, ‘Is this right for me? Or is a more traditional degree right?’ “We know this isn’t right for everyone, and so our advisors are ready to talk with prospective students, to help them think through what their career goals are, and what program best meets their needs. So, I think the conversations are starting. This is something new. I think there’s about 70 colleges around the country who are piloting these, so its still really helping people understand what it is and what it isn’t.” On the topic of other potential steps UNH is taking to reduce costs for students, VonGeorge said in terms of CPS, they’re constantly thinking through how they can help students balance work and school, and “how do we help students maximize their prior learning, so we work closely with our community college system partners on transfer pathways, so that students can bring in an associate degree right in and maximize that credit.” She said they also look closely at what kind of training certifications are happening in the workplace that are college-level learning opportunities, so that they can then give students credit for what they’ve already learned. She said they bring in students who have gone through things like police academies, fire services training and “lots of different industries.” “We have a process where they can get college credit for that learning, so that’s another opportunity for students to get credit for what they already know, and not have to retake classes for things they learned in the workplace,” she said. The Applied Bachelor of Science in Management (online) degree will help students prepare “for leadership opportunities across a variety of industries by helping them develop practical skills in leadership, project management, human resources, operations, organization, and strategic decision-making,” per the press release. The press release noted that the Applied Bachelor of Science in Computer Information Technology (online) degree helps students “build technical expertise in information systems, which includes networking, cybersecurity, virtualization, cloud computing, data management, and emerging technologies, while learning to solve real-world business and technology challenges.” VonGeorge added, “I think this is a conversation that higher education is going to continue to have. Students are thinking about stackable credentials and, ‘How do I learn what I need to know now?’ and knowing that the jobs are going to change. What you’re learning now, you have to keep learning. The workplace is evolving so rapidly that you can’t go to school and then think, ‘Okay, I’m done learning.’ This is a lifelong process.” On June 26, the University System of New Hampshire’s (USNH) Board of Trustees voted to approve consolidating the positions of both the USNH chancellor and UNH president into one role. This also would mean that the presidents of Keene State College (KSC) and Plymouth State University (PSU) would report to the consolidated position, though the two colleges will retain their independence. All three universities — UNH, KSC, and PSU — are institutions that make up USNH. The decision will now be in the hands of lawmakers during the next legislative cycle, and would require a change to a law that governs the state’s public universities. If approved, the changes could be effective as soon as July 2027, according to Lisa Thorne, director of communications for USNH. The motion which the USNH Board voted on reads: “Approval of USNH Future Leadership Recommendation moved, that, subject to statutory authorization from the State of New Hampshire, the UNH President shall assume the dual role of USNH Chancellor and UNH President on July 1, 2027; and further, that staff are directed to work with elected officials to recommend such changes to the System’s authorizing statute as are needed to allow for the permanent merging of the roles of UNH President and USNH Chancellor; and further, that the Executive Compensation and Performance Committee is hereby authorized to approve in the name of the Board any changes to the employment agreements of the UNH President and USNH Chancellor needed in order to reflect any State-approved role change.” Thorne explained that Catherine Provencher, chancellor of USNH, is set to retire on June 30, 2028, and that the Board of Trustees tasked Provencher and the university presidents with conducting research (and) returning with a recommendation on what the model should be for the university system. “The idea is that they’re collapsing two roles into one; the chancellor of the UNSH system and the UNH president would become one role. The vote was to move forward with some planning for that, but the bigger part of the vote was to empower the leadership of UNSH to work with the legislature, because the statute needs to be changed for that to move forward,” Thorne said. Thorne continued that it’s part of an ongoing efforts to streamline decision-making, and that the consolidation of roles can help lower expenses. She explained they have shared services — which includes things like human resources, administrative functions, and legal counsel across all the institutions under USNH — will also be provided by UNH starting in 2028. Thorne also said that there’s a great deal of competition for what has become fewer and fewer students graduating from high school, noting that the pool of students continues to decrease. According to a report in 2025 from the New Hampshire Department of Education, there were 162,660 students enrolled in New Hampshire public and public charter schools at the start of the 2024-2025 school year. During the 2005-2006 school year, there were more than 205,000 students enrolled in New Hampshire public and public charter schools. “There are fewer and fewer students graduating; everybody’s competing for these students, and more so, competing for the future workforce of our states… But, how do you compete? You continue having an outstanding experience for students, they get great jobs, they enjoy their experiences here and feel equipped when they leave. UNH, Plymouth State (and) Keene State are all working to do that,” Thorne said. UNH President Elizabeth S. Chilton could not be reached for comment. The company's adjusted Earnings Per Share came in at $7.23 - that's 10% better than the average prediction and a major win considering where things had been. And a Medical Care Ratio of 83.9% was way under the 85% that most people were thinking it would be So it looks like UnitedHealth Group's Q1 2026 results might signal a big shift in the way they're doing things. Instead of trying to grow as fast as possible they're now focused on getting their margins back in shape. Yes, revenue came in at $111.7 billion which is a decent 2% gain, but the real star of the show was that Earnings Per Share figure. It crushed expectations by 10% - you don't see that kind of beat very often. And that was thanks in large part to a Medical Care Ratio of 83.9%. That's a big deal because it shows they're getting better at choosing which patients to insure and how much to charge them. To do that they had to get a bit ruthless about cutting any Medicare or Medicaid memberships that wouldn't bring in a healthy profit. Management seems pretty confident about the company's future, enough so that they've bumped up their full-year Earnings Per Share forecast. That suggests they think the things they're doing now - like being more selective about who they insure - are here to stay. Even though Optum Health is still dealing with some challenges they're now looking like contained problems rather than major roadblocks. With $8.9 billion in operating cash coming in they're feeling pretty good about handing some of that back to shareholders. They're sticking to their plan to buy back at least $2 billion worth of stock by the end of the next quarter. All that said, progress on their AI-driven claims processing system is also looking pretty promising. UNH has been on a tear ever since it broke out from its base at $255, and now its testing a very important zone between $345 & $357, where a bearish trendline and a 200 day moving average are converging. The fact that the stock popped through the earnings hurdle with good volume and demand was certainly a bullish sign, but with RSI close to 80, rest assured it's over bought now. All of which adds up to a pretty solid case for buybacks and growth through AI. On the other hand, there's a bunch of reasons why UNH stock could be in for a tough time. If medical bills start to surge or if contract losses continue to be a problem for Optum Health, then the stock's got a lot of room for error. And things aren't made any easier by the fact that UNH is prioritising its profits over membership growth. That means top-line momentum is pretty limited, so investors are going to have to keep a close eye on the Q2 MCR - that'll really be the deciding factor as to whether Q1 was a one-off or the start of a trend. Well, it was a pretty strong set of numbers - the EPS was up by 8% and came in at $7.23, beating forecasts by about 10%. title: UNH Stock: UnitedHealth Roared Back With a Q2 Blowout — but Is It Still a Buy After the Rally? - top1markets.com
content: Dear user, to protect your funds, please stay vigilant and beware of the following scams: Stay alert and trade with peace of mind! Twelve months ago, UNH stock was a falling knife. Elevated medical costs gutted margins, management cut guidance more than once, and shares collapsed from over $460 to the mid-$240s. Then the story flipped. On July 16, 2026, UnitedHealth reported second-quarter earnings that crushed Wall Street's estimates, raised its full-year profit outlook, and sent the stock on a run that has it up roughly 60% over the past year. As of the August 7 close, UNH traded near $407, hovering around $410 in early August as it consolidates the July surge. The question every investor is now asking: after a rebound this sharp, is UNH stock still a buy — or has the easy money already been made? The numbers were emphatic. UnitedHealth posted Q2 revenue of $112.0 billion (just ahead of the roughly $110.8 billion consensus) and adjusted earnings of $6.38 per share — obliterating the ~$4.85–$4.91 the Street expected and up 56% from $4.08 a year earlier. Reported GAAP EPS was $6.04, with net income of $5.48 billion, and operating earnings jumped 55% year over year to $8.0 billion. The single most important figure was the medical care ratio (MCR), which fell to 86.7% from 89.4% a year earlier — well below the ~88.5% analysts feared. That drop is what markets cheered: it signaled that the runaway Medicare Advantage utilization that haunted the stock for over a year is finally normalizing. Roughly $860 million of favorable prior-period development helped, but pricing discipline and benefit redesign did the heavy lifting. Management then raised full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $19.50–$20.00 (from a prior floor above $18.25), lifted the buyback target to at least $5 billion, and kept revenue guidance above $439 billion, with the CFO signaling it could come in higher. Here's the tension. At around $410 against the midpoint of guidance (~$19.75), UNH trades near 20 times forward earnings — reasonable for a scaled, cash-generative healthcare compounder, and below where the stock changed hands in its pre-crisis years. Many analysts lifted price targets after the print, with several bull cases pointing to the mid-$450s, implying double-digit upside if the recovery holds. The dividend, raised to an annualized ~$9.28 (a ~2.2% yield), plus a beefed-up buyback, sweeten the total-return case. The counterweight is expectations. The stock has already repriced a lot of good news, and the next catalyst — Q3 earnings, tentatively early October — carries a consensus near $3.74 in EPS. That's a steep step-down from $6.38, but it's mechanical, not deterioration: UnitedHealth front-loads roughly two-thirds of its earnings into the first half, so the sequential drop is baked into the annual shape. The risk is that a market anchored on the Q2 beat reacts to the smaller headline number rather than the full-year trajectory. In practice, "is it a buy" comes down to whether you believe the margin recovery is durable — because at 20x forward earnings, the stock is priced for it to continue, not to re-accelerate. This is the crux, and the honest answer is that it's a multi-year repair, not a one-quarter fix. Three things support durability. First, UnitedHealth is deliberately choosing margin over membership: UnitedHealthcare served 48.5 million people, down 525,000 from the prior quarter, and management expects to shed roughly 500,000 ACA and 1.1 million Medicare Advantage members this year — yet premium increases are large enough to keep revenue roughly flat. Walking away from unprofitable contracts is exactly how a payer rebuilds its loss ratio. Second, Optum keeps compounding: the health-services arm generated $65.7 billion in revenue and $4.0 billion in operating earnings, expanding margins by 160 basis points year over year and serving more than 120 million consumers. Third, management is leaning on cost discipline and AI-driven efficiency to streamline operations. The caution: full-year MCR guidance sits around 88.1%, above the 86.7% Q2 print, which tells you management itself expects some give-back as seasonal costs land and commercial trends stay elevated. Guidance credibility is improving after a rough 2025, but the company has to keep clearing the bar it just raised. The biggest overhang isn't operational — it's legal. UnitedHealth faces ongoing Department of Justice civil and criminal investigations into its Medicare Advantage practices, particularly around risk-adjustment coding and billing. That is a genuine tail risk that no earnings beat resolves, and headlines on it can move the stock regardless of fundamentals. Layered on top are broader policy risks — Medicare Advantage funding rates, scrutiny of prior-authorization and AI use in coverage decisions — plus the ever-present chance that medical cost trends reaccelerate. Against peers, UNH's edge is scale and diversification: Optum gives it a services-and-data engine that pure insurers like Humana lack, while Elevance, Cigna, and CVS Health (Aetna) each carry their own margin and integration challenges. For long-term holders, the bull thesis is a wide-moat compounder restoring normalized margins with heavy cash returns; the bear thesis is a regulated business with a DOJ cloud, shrinking membership, and a stock that has already run 60%. Both can be true at once — which is why the sensible posture is to treat the Q3 report and any DOJ developments as the checkpoints, rather than chasing the rebound blindly. Q1: Is UNH stock a buy after Q2 2026 earnings?A1: It depends on your read of durability. At ~$410, UNH trades near 20x forward earnings with raised guidance ($19.50–$20.00), a ~2.2% dividend, and a ≥$5B buyback — attractive if the margin recovery holds. The offsetting risks are an ongoing DOJ investigation and a stock that's already up ~60% in a year. This is analysis, not advice. Q2: Why did UNH stock crash in 2025 and recover in 2026?A2: In 2025, elevated Medicare Advantage medical costs compressed margins and forced repeated guidance cuts, sending shares to the mid-$240s. In 2026, tighter cost management, pricing actions, and exits from unprofitable contracts pushed the medical care ratio down and earnings up, driving the rebound. Q3: What is UnitedHealth's medical care ratio and why does it matter?A3: The medical care ratio (MCR) is the share of every premium dollar spent on medical claims — lower is better for margins. UNH's Q2 MCR fell to 86.7% from 89.4% a year earlier, the key signal that utilization is normalizing. Q4: What are the biggest risks to UNH stock right now?A4: The DOJ's civil and criminal investigations into its Medicare Advantage practices, potential policy/funding changes, a possible reacceleration in medical costs, and the risk that the market over-reacts to the seasonally lower Q3 earnings. On July 29, UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH) announced a $4 million commitment, funded through the United Health Foundation, to expand the University of Tennessee Health Sciences' health hub network from 5 locations to 13 across the state by the end of 2027, a buildout expected to reach 200,000 Tennessee residents. It's a modest sum for a company this size, but it lands as UnitedHealth works to repair a business that fell apart just a year earlier. The repair is showing up in the numbers. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio, the share of premiums spent on claims, hit 88.9% in 2025, up from 85.5% in 2024, and operating earnings collapsed from $32 billion to $19 billion as a result. That ratio has since started reversing: it came in at 86.7% in the second quarter, below the 88.5% analysts expected, and management is now guiding to 88% for the full year while aiming to beat it. Second-quarter revenue of $112 billion topped the $110.9 billion analysts projected, and adjusted earnings per share of $6.38 came in well above the $4.90 consensus estimate. UnitedHealth followed that quarter by raising its full-year adjusted EPS guidance to a range of $19.50 to $20, up from its prior forecast of $18.25. The company has also credited restructuring, including exiting unprofitable contracts, and new use of AI to speed up processes. UnitedHealth's revenue has grown 150% over the past 10 years, a run one analysis tied to healthcare spending rising faster than the economy. The stock has climbed nearly 50% over the past year as the turnaround has taken hold. Not every signal points the same way. Berkshire Hathaway bought UnitedHealth stock at an average price around $380 in the second quarter of 2025 and exited the position in the first quarter of 2026 at less than $300, one of the conglomerate's rare recent losses. On a trailing basis, the stock still isn't cheap: at a market cap of $380 billion against trailing net income of $14.9 billion, UnitedHealth carries a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 25.5, a multiple that assumes the margin recovery continues rather than stalls. One analysis put shares at 23 times estimated future earnings and noted the stock would need to climb roughly another 19% to revisit the $500 level it hasn't traded at since early last year, a bar that leaves little room for the medical care ratio to disappoint the way it did in 2025. UnitedHealth trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 20.58 as of August 7, a discount to its 25.5 trailing multiple, and a sign the market expects the medical care ratio recovery to continue. Short interest sits at a modest 2.13% of the float, suggesting limited organized betting against the turnaround. The hedge fund count tied to the stock fell from 145 to 130 quarter over quarter, a pullback that runs counter to the stock's rebound. UnitedHealth's Tennessee expansion is a small piece of a much larger story: a company trying to prove that 2025's earnings collapse was a pricing problem it has since fixed, not a permanent shift in its cost structure.
